passage: In Gurpreet's village near Moga, people said you saw a doctor for fever and a granthi for worries. After her engagement broke off, she stopped sleeping and lost interest in the dairy work she loved. Her cousin Vandana, a nurse in the district hospital, visited on a Sunday. "There's a counsellor at the hospital on Thursdays," she said. Gurpreet laughed. "I'm not mad." Vandana shrugged. "You get your tractor serviced before it breaks. Same idea." Gurpreet thought about it all week. On Thursday she took the bus, a dupatta pulled over her face in case someone saw. The counsellor was a calm woman who mostly listened. Gurpreet went back three more times. She stopped hiding her face by the second visit.

qa.q: On which day was the counsellor at the hospital?
qa.a: The counsellor was there on Thursdays.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet pull her dupatta over her face on the bus?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and worried people would judge her for seeing a counsellor.

qa.q: What made Vandana's way of suggesting help effective?
qa.a: She compared counselling to routine tractor servicing, making it feel ordinary rather than a sign of being 'mad'.

qa.q: What would change if more people in the village saw counselling like Vandana does?
qa.a: People like Gurpreet might seek help sooner without hiding, because it would feel as normal as seeing a doctor.

grounding: Shows a young woman in a village coming to see counselling as ordinary care and choosing it despite stigma.

passage: Liam had been in Dublin eight months, working long hours at a design agency. He wasn't in crisis, just flat, snappy, and waking at four every morning. His flatmate Siddiq mentioned that he saw a therapist every other week. "For what?" Liam asked. "Nothing's wrong with you." Siddiq smiled. "That's sort of the point. I go so things don't get bad." Liam looked into his company's employee support scheme and found six free sessions. He wasn't sure whether he needed a therapist, a doctor or just more sleep, so he asked his GP first, who suggested talking therapy. The first session felt awkward. By the third, Liam noticed he was sleeping until six. He booked three more.

qa.q: How many free sessions did Liam's company scheme offer?
qa.a: It offered six free sessions.

qa.q: Why did Liam ask Siddiq 'For what?'
qa.a: He was surprised, because he believed therapy was only for people with something clearly wrong.

qa.q: What was sensible about how Liam chose his help?
qa.a: He wasn't sure what kind of support he needed, so he asked his GP first and then used the free sessions.

qa.q: How does Siddiq see therapy differently from Liam at first?
qa.a: Siddiq sees it as regular upkeep to stop problems growing, not as a last resort. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young man treating therapy as routine care and choosing suitable help through a doctor.

passage: The staff wellness room at the Jaipur software firm had a sign-up sheet for peer support circles on Wednesdays. Simran walked past it for a month. After a bad quarter and a breakup, she finally wrote her name down. Lalit from accounts ran the circle; he'd trained as a peer listener after his own rough year. "This isn't therapy," he said at the start. "It's people listening. If anyone needs more, I'll help you find a counsellor." Simran mostly listened the first week. In the second, she spoke about feeling like she was failing at everything. Afterward Lalit quietly gave her the card for the company's counselling service. She booked a session, relieved that it was both.

qa.q: On which day did the peer support circles meet?
qa.a: They met on Wednesdays.

qa.q: What might Simran walking past the sheet for a month suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was hesitant, perhaps unsure she needed help or worried what others would think.

qa.q: What made Lalit's circle a safe choice for Simran?
qa.a: He was clear about what the circle could and couldn't do, and pointed her to a counsellor when she needed more.

qa.q: How might Lalit see his role in the circle?
qa.a: He sees himself as a listener and a bridge to professional help, not a therapist, drawing on his own rough year.

grounding: Shows a young worker using peer support at work as ordinary care and being guided to counselling when needed.

passage:
Dear Tanuja,

You asked why I seemed so tired at Diwali. Here's the truth.

I'm a son who's expected to run Appa's printing shop in Madurai, a husband to you, and a teacher who loves his students in Chennai. For two years I tried to be all three fully and felt like I was lying to everyone.

Last month I wrote down what I actually value: teaching, family, honest work. Then I told Appa I won't take over the shop, but I'll help him find a manager and come home one weekend a month to check the books.

He was quiet for a long time. Then he asked if I'd teach his assistant accounts. That felt like a door, not a wall.

I'm still working it out. But I don't feel split anymore.

Shankar

qa.q: Which city is the printing shop in?
qa.a: The printing shop is in Madurai.

qa.q: What does Shankar mean by feeling 'like I was lying to everyone'?
qa.a: He felt torn between roles, pretending to give each one his full self when he couldn't.

qa.q: What made Shankar's solution fit his values?
qa.a: He kept teaching, stayed involved in the family business in a smaller way and was honest with his father.

qa.q: How might Shankar's father have felt during his long silence?
qa.a: He may have felt disappointed and sad, but asking Shankar to teach his assistant showed he was accepting it.

grounding: Shows a young man reconciling family duty, marriage and work into an identity that fits his values.

passage: This is something I've been thinking about. At twenty-five I had a finance job, a fiancée my family chose, and a secret. Every weekend I volunteered with a theatre group, and I felt more like myself there than anywhere. I told nobody at home. My friend Manoj said, 'You're living two lives, Akash. Which one's yours?' I got angry with him. But he wasn't wrong. So I started small. I told my fiancée first. She laughed and said she already knew, she'd seen photos. Then I told my parents. My father thought it was a waste of time. I didn't quit my job. I just stopped hiding. Now I'm one man, not two. It's messier, but it's mine.

qa.q: Where did Akash volunteer every weekend?
qa.a: He volunteered with a theatre group.

qa.q: Why did Akash get angry with Manoj?
qa.a: Manoj's comment touched something true that Akash wasn't ready to face, so it stung.

qa.q: What small step helped Akash stop living two lives?
qa.a: He told people one at a time, starting with his fiancée, instead of hiding his theatre work.

qa.q: How did Akash's fiancée react differently from his father?
qa.a: She laughed and already knew, while his father saw the theatre as a waste of time.

grounding: Shows a young man bringing his hidden values and his family-shaped life together into one identity.

passage: I'm Nirmala, Kavitha's aunt. Kavitha grew up in our joint family in Mysuru, the good daughter who never argued. At twenty-four she became a lawyer in Bengaluru, took cases for tenants facing eviction, and started missing family functions. My sister complained she'd changed. Last month she came home for a cousin's wedding. She helped cook, sat with her grandmother, and wore the silk sari her mother wanted. At dinner an uncle mocked her 'poor clients'. She put her spoon down and said calmly, 'They're people like us, Mama.' Then she went back to eating. I don't know what she felt inside. But she seemed to be both things at once, the daughter and the lawyer, without apologising for either.

qa.q: What kind of cases does Kavitha take?
qa.a: She takes cases for tenants facing eviction.

qa.q: What might Kavitha putting her spoon down before answering suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt the uncle's mockery strongly but chose to answer calmly instead of angrily.

qa.q: What is wise about how Kavitha handled the wedding visit?
qa.a: She joined in family duties and customs while still standing up for her values when challenged.

qa.q: How does Nirmala see Kavitha's change?
qa.a: Nirmala sees her as someone who has joined her roles together, though she admits she can't know Kavitha's inner feelings.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a young woman hold family duty and her work values together in one identity.

passage: I'm Madhuri, and I've worked with Abhinav at the logistics startup for two years. Last spring he had to decide whether to open a new warehouse in Nagpur. The demand numbers were patchy and nobody could say for sure. I watched him list what he knew and what he didn't, then decide to rent a small space for six months instead of buying a big one. "If I'm wrong, we lose less," he said. Three months in, orders came in lower than hoped. He didn't panic or blame the data team. He adjusted the plan and moved some stock back. Later he said, "It was a reasonable bet that didn't pay off fully." I'm not sure I could stay that calm.

qa.q: Which city was the new warehouse in?
qa.a: It was in Nagpur.

qa.q: What does Abhinav's calm after the low orders suggest about how he felt about uncertainty?
qa.a: He planned for being wrong by renting small, and later called it a reasonable bet instead of blaming anyone.

qa.q: What made Abhinav's decision good even though orders came in low?
qa.a: He decided with the information he had, limited the risk and adjusted when new facts arrived.

qa.q: How does Madhuri see Abhinav's calm?
qa.a: Madhuri admires it and doubts being able to stay that calm.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a colleague decide with incomplete data, update his plan and accept an uncertain outcome.

passage:
Monday: Vishal's aunt Nirmala was offered a transfer to Guwahati. She asked him, the family's 'planner', to help decide. He wanted certainty and asked for more information from everyone.

Thursday: More information only made things muddier. The school fees were higher, but the pay was better. Vishal realised they'd never be sure. He suggested listing the three things that mattered most and estimating how likely each outcome was. His aunt laughed. "You sound like a weather forecaster."

Three weeks later: She took the transfer. The first month was hard; her son hated the new school. Vishal worried he'd pushed wrongly. But his aunt said, "We decided well with what we knew. Now we adjust." By the second month, her son had a friend.

qa.q: Where was Nirmala offered a transfer?
qa.a: She was offered a transfer to Guwahati.

qa.q: Why did Vishal worry after the move?
qa.a: He feared his advice had pushed his aunt into a bad decision when her son hated the new school.

qa.q: What approach helped the family decide under uncertainty?
qa.a: Listing what mattered most and estimating likely outcomes, then adjusting after the choice was made.

qa.q: How does Nirmala see a hard first month differently from Vishal?
qa.a: She sees it as part of the risk of a good decision, not proof that the decision was wrong.

grounding: Shows a young man learning to decide with incomplete information and accept that outcomes can vary.

passage: Mohit, sit down, I'll tell you about my shop. I was twenty-six when I had to choose: sell cloth in our old market or open near the new bus stand. Nobody knew if the bus stand would bring customers. My father said stay. My friend said go. I couldn't know. So I did something my father thought was mad. I kept the old shop and rented a tiny counter near the bus stand for one season. I watched who came, what they bought. The counter did better. The next year I moved. Some years were good, some bad. You can make a good choice and still have a bad year, beta. I'm Naveen-dada to you, but back then I was just a scared young man guessing carefully.

qa.q: Where did Naveen rent a tiny counter?
qa.a: He rented it near the new bus stand.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel when he had to choose?
qa.a: He felt scared and unsure, since nobody could tell him whether the bus stand would bring customers.

qa.q: What lesson could Mohit take from Naveen's story?
qa.a: When you can't know the outcome, test with a small step and learn before making a big move.

qa.q: How might Naveen's father have seen the counter idea?
qa.a: He thought it was mad, probably because he preferred the safety of the old market.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how he tested a decision under uncertainty and accepted that good choices can have bad years.

subtype: Managing Anger, Envy & Ego at Work
passage: At the cooperative sugar factory near Kolhapur, Pradeep had trained Indu when she joined. Two years later she was made shift supervisor, not him. He heard it at the tea stall and felt his face burn. That evening he snapped at his younger brother over nothing. At night he lay awake, thinking of every mistake she'd ever made. The next morning he nearly skipped her first meeting. Instead he went, sat at the back and said little. Afterward he walked by the cane fields and admitted to himself that she was good at planning, better than him. He congratulated her the next day, stiffly. She said, "You taught me half of it." His chest loosened a little.

qa.q: Where did Pradeep hear about Indu's promotion?
qa.a: He heard it at the tea stall.

qa.q: What does Pradeep lying awake thinking of Indu's mistakes suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt envious and hurt, looking for reasons she didn't deserve the promotion.

qa.q: How did Pradeep manage his envy professionally?
qa.a: He attended her meeting, reflected honestly on her strengths and congratulated her, even if stiffly.

qa.q: How might Indu have seen Pradeep's congratulations?
qa.a: She probably noticed the stiffness but valued it, and her reply showed she respected him.

grounding: Shows a young man handling envy and hurt pride after a colleague's promotion in a professional way.

subtype: Managing Anger, Envy & Ego at Work
passage: Rosa had worked at the Lima architecture firm longer than Bao, but it was Bao's design the partners chose for the library project. In the meeting, Rosa smiled and clapped. In the bathroom afterward, she gripped the sink and breathed. She wanted to point out, loudly, that his design ignored drainage. Instead, she waited until the next morning, calmer. She wrote Bao a short message: "Congrats. One thing to check, the drainage on the east side might flood in heavy rain. Happy to help." Bao replied, "You're right, I missed that. Can we look together?" They spent an afternoon on it. Rosa still felt a pinch when the partners praised him. But the building would be better.

qa.q: Which project did the partners choose Bao's design for?
qa.a: They chose it for the library project.

qa.q: What was Rosa feeling when she gripped the sink?
qa.a: She felt envious and angry, and was trying to calm herself before reacting.

qa.q: What made Rosa's handling of her feelings professional?
qa.a: She waited until she was calm and raised a real problem helpfully instead of attacking Bao in front of others.

qa.q: How might Bao see Rosa after her message?
qa.a: He probably sees her as generous and skilled, since he welcomed her help.

grounding: Shows a young architect managing envy and ego after a rival's success by acting professionally.

subtype: Managing Anger, Envy & Ego at Work
passage: In the break room of the city hospital's billing department, Nazia heard a colleague say that Rekha, the new manager, had been hired because she was the director's niece. Nazia had applied for the same job. Her ears went hot. For days she was curt with Rekha and rolled her eyes in meetings. Then Rekha asked to speak with her privately. "I know you wanted this role," Rekha said. "I'd value your experience. Can you lead the new system training?" Nazia wanted to stay angry. Instead she said, "Okay. And I'm sorry I've been rude." She never found out if the rumour was true. She decided to judge Rekha by her work instead.

qa.q: Where did Nazia hear the rumour about Rekha?
qa.a: She heard it in the break room of the billing department.

qa.q: Why was Nazia curt with Rekha for days?
qa.a: She was envious and hurt about missing the job, and the rumour fed her anger.

qa.q: What helped Nazia move past her anger?
qa.a: Rekha's respectful offer gave her a real role, and Nazia chose to apologise and judge Rekha by her work.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt about Nazia's eye-rolling?
qa.a: She likely noticed and felt the tension, but chose to address it privately and with respect.

grounding: Shows a young worker moving from envy and rivalry to professional conduct after missing a promotion.

passage: Thomas had four hours to submit a market report to a client in Nairobi, and the office printer and half the network were down. He used an AI writing tool to draft the summary from his data. It was fast and fluent. His colleague Pallavi glanced at it. "That growth figure looks odd." Thomas checked: the tool had made up a number that wasn't in his data. His stomach dropped. With the clock ticking, he went through every figure, line by line, against the spreadsheet. Two more were wrong. He fixed them and added a note that AI had helped draft the text but he had verified the numbers. He sent it with twenty minutes to spare. He told Pallavi, "I owe you tea."

qa.q: What did the AI tool make up in the report?
qa.a: It made up a growth figure that wasn't in his data.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when he found the made-up number?
qa.a: He felt a jolt of fear, as his stomach dropped, realising he'd almost sent false data.

qa.q: What did Thomas do right under time pressure?
qa.a: He checked every figure against the spreadsheet, fixed errors and was open about using AI while staying responsible for the numbers.

qa.q: What would have happened if Pallavi hadn't glanced at the report?
qa.a: The client might have received false figures, damaging trust in Thomas and his firm.

grounding: Shows a young professional using AI under pressure while verifying results and keeping accountability.

passage: Sahil, a junior developer at a Pune software firm, had started using an AI assistant to write most of his code. His team lead, Pankaj, noticed Sahil's pull requests getting bigger and faster. One afternoon Pankaj asked him to explain a function line by line. Sahil couldn't. His ears went red. "The AI wrote it," he mumbled. Pankaj didn't scold him. "Use it, it's useful. But if you can't explain it, you can't own it." They agreed that Sahil would write core logic himself each Friday, and use AI for tests and boilerplate. He would also review every AI suggestion before committing. After a month, Sahil caught an AI bug in someone else's code during review. He felt proud.

qa.q: On which day would Sahil write core logic himself?
qa.a: He would write it himself each Friday.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when he couldn't explain the function?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed; his ears went red and he mumbled his answer.

qa.q: What balance did Sahil and Pankaj agree on?
qa.a: Sahil would use AI for tests and boilerplate, write core logic himself on Fridays and review every AI suggestion.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see the AI assistant?
qa.a: He sees it as a useful tool but insists the developer must understand and own the code it produces. 👍

grounding: Shows a young developer learning to delegate to AI while keeping accountability and protecting his own skills.

passage:
"Sudha-di, look. I made the whole school newsletter in ten minutes with the AI tool!"
"Ten minutes? Hansa, did you read it?"
"Mostly. Why?"
"Because it says the annual day is on the fifteenth. It's on the twelfth."
"Oh no. It must have guessed."
"And this quote from the principal. Did she say that?"
"...I don't think so."
"So it made it up."
"I just wanted to save time. I have forty copies to print tonight."
"Save time, fine. But your name's on it, not the tool's."
"So I check every fact?"
"Every date, every name, every quote. And write the principal's message yourself. You're good at that."
"Okay. Twenty minutes, not ten. Still faster than before."

qa.q: What date is the annual day actually on?
qa.a: It is on the twelfth.

qa.q: How was Hansa feeling while relying on the AI tool for the newsletter?
qa.a: Hansa was feeling rushed and pressured, with forty copies to print that night, and excited to finish in ten minutes.

qa.q: What rule does Sudha suggest for using AI tools?
qa.a: Check every date, name and quote, and write the personal parts yourself, because you are responsible for what goes out.

qa.q: What would change if Hansa printed the newsletter unchecked?
qa.a: Parents would get the wrong date and a fake quote, which could confuse them and embarrass the principal and Hansa.

grounding: Shows a young teacher learning to verify AI output and keep responsibility for what goes out.

passage: The video arrived in Sarika's family group on a Tuesday morning: a well-known local doctor in Indore saying a common vaccine caused illness. Her uncle had already forwarded it to twelve people. Sarika, who worked in a newsroom, watched it twice. The lips didn't quite match the words, and the doctor's earrings changed between frames. She called her colleague Vidya, who handled fact-checks. Vidya found the original clip in ten minutes; the doctor had been talking about something else entirely. Sarika posted the original link in the family group with a gentle note. Her uncle replied, "How can you be sure?" She explained the earrings. There was a long pause, then he deleted his forward and wrote, "Thank you, beta."

qa.q: How many people had Sarika's uncle forwarded the video to?
qa.a: He had forwarded it to twelve people.

qa.q: What might her uncle's long pause before deleting the forward suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt embarrassed or unsettled at having been fooled, before accepting the evidence.

qa.q: What steps did Sarika take before challenging the video?
qa.a: She watched it carefully, noticed mismatches, asked a fact-checker and found the original clip before posting.

qa.q: How might the doctor be affected by the fake video spreading?
qa.a: The doctor's reputation could be harmed and people might lose trust in real health advice.

grounding: Shows a young journalist detecting a manipulated video and verifying it before correcting family members.

passage:
"Tanuja, don't share that!"
"Why? It's a news clip. The minister said schools will close for a month."
"Did he? Where's it from?"
"A forward. It looks real."
"Looks real isn't the same as real. Check the government site."
"Ugh, Nilesh, you're so suspicious."
"I work in cybersecurity. I have to be."
"...Fine. The site says nothing about closures."
"And the news channels?"
"Nothing either. Oh. So it's fake?"
"Maybe edited, or an old clip. Either way, it's not confirmed."
"I almost sent it to the parents' group. Forty people."
"Then forty people would panic. Maybe post that it's unverified instead?"
"Yeah. Doing that now."

qa.q: How many people are in the parents' group?
qa.a: There are forty people in the parents' group.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel on realising the clip might be fake?
qa.a: Tanuja was surprised and a bit shaken, realising the clip almost went to forty people.

qa.q: What verification steps did Nilesh suggest?
qa.a: Checking the government website and news channels before trusting or sharing the clip.

qa.q: If you were a parent in that group, what would you want?
qa.a: You'd want to be warned the clip was unverified, rather than panic over a fake school closure.

grounding: Shows two young adults checking official sources before sharing a possibly fake news clip.

passage: Last month someone sent me a voice note that sounded exactly like my friend Nazia, crying, saying she'd been arrested in Dubai and needed money fast. My heart was pounding. I actually opened my banking app. Then something small bothered me. She called me 'Jaya-ji'. Nazia has never called me that in fifteen years. I hung up and called Nazia's real number. She answered from her office in Hyderabad, confused. It was a cloned voice. I felt sick thinking how close I came. I reported the number to the cybercrime helpline and warned our friends' group. Now Nazia and I have a silly code word. It feels a bit dramatic. But I'd rather feel dramatic than fooled.

qa.q: Where was Nazia actually when Jaya called her?
qa.a: She was at her office in Hyderabad.

qa.q: What made Jaya suspicious of the voice note?
qa.a: The voice said 'Jaya-ji', which the real Nazia never does, so something felt wrong despite the panic.

qa.q: What smart steps did Jaya take after hanging up?
qa.a: Jaya called Nazia's real number, reported the scam number to the cybercrime helpline and warned their friends.

qa.q: How might Nazia have felt learning her voice was cloned?
qa.a: She was probably confused and uneasy that her voice could be used to trick her friends.

grounding: Shows a young woman spotting a cloned-voice scam and verifying before acting.

passage: Madhav ran a small agricultural supply shop in a town near Hubli. His phone buzzed all day with group chats, videos and news alerts. One evening he realised he'd spent two hours watching short clips and forgotten to call a farmer back about seeds. His friend Eshaan, a schoolteacher, had deleted most apps from his own phone. "I kept only what I need," Eshaan said. "Business chat, bank, weather." Madhav tried it. He muted twenty groups, deleted the video app and put his phone in a drawer after nine. The first week felt restless; he kept reaching for it. By the third week he'd read half a book on soil health. Business calls got returned the same day.

qa.q: How long had Madhav spent watching short clips that evening?
qa.a: He had spent two hours watching them.

qa.q: What does Madhav keep reaching for his phone in the first week suggest?
qa.a: It suggests his habit was strong and he felt restless without constant updates.

qa.q: What made Madhav's changes effective?
qa.a: He removed apps he didn't need, muted distracting groups and set a time for the phone to go away.

qa.q: How might the farmers Madhav works with see this change?
qa.a: They'd likely notice he calls back faster and seems more attentive, which builds trust. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young shopkeeper choosing his technology deliberately instead of by default.

passage: Kaito, a graphic designer in Osaka, noticed he checked the news every time he waited for a file to render. He felt anxious and scattered by lunchtime. His colleague Nadia had a different system: she read one weekly news summary on Sunday and nothing else. "Isn't that out of touch?" Kaito asked. "I miss nothing important," she said. "Important things are still there on Sunday." Kaito tried a milder version. He removed news apps, kept one trusted source he read in the evening, and set his phone to grayscale during work. The first days he felt left out of office chatter. After a month, he found he could hold a design idea in his head for an hour without losing it.

qa.q: When does Nadia read her weekly news summary?
qa.a: She reads it on Sunday.

qa.q: How did Kaito feel before changing his habits?
qa.a: He felt anxious and scattered by lunchtime from checking news constantly.

qa.q: What choices did Kaito make to use technology more deliberately?
qa.a: He removed news apps, kept one trusted source for evenings and set his phone to grayscale at work.

qa.q: How does Nadia see keeping up with the news?
qa.a: She believes important news will still be there on Sunday, so constant checking isn't necessary.

grounding: Shows a young designer choosing his information diet consciously after seeing a colleague's approach.

passage: At the engineering firm's weekly team meeting, Vaibhav noticed everyone, including himself, was typing on laptops while someone presented. Nobody remembered decisions afterward. As the newest team lead, he proposed an experiment: laptops closed in meetings except for the note-taker, and messages answered in two batches a day instead of instantly. Akash, the senior engineer, scoffed. "Clients expect quick replies." "Urgent calls still come through," Vaibhav said. "Let's try two weeks." The first week was awkward; people fidgeted. By the second, meetings ended fifteen minutes early. Akash admitted he'd finished a design he'd been stuck on for a month. He didn't say thanks. But he started closing his laptop without being asked.

qa.q: How often would messages be answered in Vaibhav's experiment?
qa.a: They would be answered in two batches a day.

qa.q: Why did Akash scoff at the proposal at first?
qa.a: He worried that clients would be unhappy if replies weren't quick.

qa.q: What made Vaibhav's experiment easier for the team to accept?
qa.a: He framed it as a short two-week trial and kept urgent calls open, so people didn't feel cut off.

qa.q: How did Akash's view seem to change?
qa.a: After finishing a stuck design, he quietly began closing his laptop in meetings, showing he saw the benefit.

grounding: Shows a young team lead introducing deliberate tech habits at work and colleagues slowly adopting them.

passage:
January: Tenzin and his wife Gopika sat with their rent receipts in their Pune flat. Relatives kept asking when they'd buy a house. Tenzin felt behind everyone.

March: They met a fee-only financial adviser recommended by a colleague. She showed them how buying and renting each had costs people forget, like maintenance, interest and being tied to one city. Gopika's job might move. They decided to keep renting for now and build savings.

October: They checked their health cover was enough for both of them and started small, regular retirement contributions. At Diwali, an uncle asked again about a house. Tenzin smiled. "Not yet. We have a plan." For the first time, he didn't feel behind.

qa.q: Whom did Tenzin and Gopika meet in March?
qa.a: They met a fee-only financial adviser recommended by a colleague.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel in January, and why?
qa.a: He felt pressured and behind everyone, because relatives kept asking when they would buy a house.

qa.q: What made their decision a thoughtful one?
qa.a: They got professional advice, compared the hidden costs of buying and renting, and considered Gopika's possible job move.

qa.q: How might relatives see the couple's choice to keep renting?
qa.a: Some may think they're falling behind, not knowing the couple has a clear plan for their future.

grounding: Shows a young couple comparing renting and buying, checking insurance and starting retirement saving over a year.

passage: Tushar, beta, listen to your old Siddharth-mama. When I was twenty-five, I thought retirement was for old men. I spent everything: new scooter, trips, dinners. My friend started putting a little aside every month and I laughed at him. Thirty years later, he retired calmly. I had to keep working longer than I planned. It wasn't a tragedy, but I was tired. And when your mami fell ill, we had no health insurance. The hospital bills took years to pay. So when you get your first salary, talk to someone trustworthy about insurance and a small savings plan for later. Not because I'm telling you. Because I wish someone had told me.

qa.q: What did Siddharth-mama spend his money on at twenty-five?
qa.a: He spent it on a new scooter, trips and dinners.

qa.q: How does Siddharth-mama feel looking back on his choices?
qa.a: He feels regretful and tired, wishing someone had warned him to plan earlier.

qa.q: What does he advise Tushar to do with his first salary?
qa.a: Talk to someone trustworthy about insurance and a small savings plan for later.

qa.q: How might Siddharth-mama's friend see his own early choice?
qa.a: He likely feels glad that saving a little each month let him retire calmly.

grounding: Shows an elder urging a young relative to think early about insurance and retirement saving.

passage: Gargi and Ojas had one week to decide on a flat in Kochi before the builder's offer expired. The monsoon had flooded their current rented place twice. The builder's brochure was glossy, and a relative pushed them to sign quickly. Gargi insisted they slow down. They visited the site in the rain and saw water pooling near the basement. They asked a lawyer friend to check the documents and learned the building approvals weren't complete. Ojas was frustrated. "We'll lose the chance!" But Gargi calmly listed what they didn't know. They decided to keep renting another year, and moved to a higher-floor flat. The offer expired. Ojas sulked for a day, then admitted he felt relieved.

qa.q: What did Gargi and Ojas see at the site in the rain?
qa.a: They saw water pooling near the basement.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he said 'We'll lose the chance!'?
qa.a: He was frustrated and anxious that they would miss out on owning a flat.

qa.q: What made Gargi's approach sensible under time pressure?
qa.a: Gargi checked the site in bad weather and had documents reviewed before committing, refusing to be rushed.

qa.q: How might the pushy relative see their decision?
qa.a: They might think the couple missed a good chance, not knowing about the flooding and incomplete approvals.

grounding: Shows a young couple resisting pressure to buy a home and comparing risks before deciding to keep renting.

passage:
Month one: Vinita got a big raise at her design firm in Mumbai. That weekend she bought a new phone, booked a fancy dinner and started taking cabs everywhere.

Month four: Her savings hadn't grown at all. Her brother Naveen asked, half joking, "Where does all your money go?" She checked her statements that night and felt a little sick. Most of it went to things she barely remembered buying.

Month eight: She had set up an automatic transfer to savings on payday, before she could spend it. She kept one treat a month, the dinner with friends she actually enjoyed, and went back to the metro on most days. When a colleague showed off a designer bag, Vinita felt a tug. She admired it, then let it go.

qa.q: What did Vinita start taking everywhere after her raise?
qa.a: She started taking cabs everywhere.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel when she checked her statements?
qa.a: She felt a little sick and dismayed, realising most of her money went on things she barely remembered.

qa.q: What helped Vinita keep spending below her income growth?
qa.a: Automatically moving savings on payday, keeping one treat she valued and cutting habits she didn't care about.

qa.q: How might Naveen see his sister's changes?
qa.a: He might feel pleased that his half-joking question helped her take control of her money.

grounding: Shows a young woman noticing lifestyle inflation after a raise and changing her spending over months.

passage: Sarika, my child, sit with your Alka-aunty for a minute. When your uncle got his first big promotion, we moved to a bigger flat, bought a car on loan and started going to expensive weddings with expensive gifts. Everyone thought we were doing well. Inside, we were always worried about the next bill. One night I sat on the kitchen floor and cried over the car loan. Your uncle held my hand and said, 'Who are we doing this for?' It was a good question. We sold the car, moved somewhere smaller and gave simpler gifts. Some relatives gossiped. We slept better. Now you're earning well. Enjoy it, but ask yourself that question often.

qa.q: What did Alka and her husband buy on loan?
qa.a: They bought a car on loan.

qa.q: What does crying on the kitchen floor tell you about how Alka felt?
qa.a: It shows she was deeply stressed and worried, despite looking successful to others.

qa.q: What question does Alka want Sarika to keep asking?
qa.a: 'Who are we doing this for?' — so Sarika can separate real needs from spending to impress others.

qa.q: How did relatives see the couple's simpler life?
qa.a: Some gossiped, probably thinking the couple had fallen on hard times.

grounding: Shows an elder sharing how spending for image caused stress and how simpler choices helped.

passage: Bidisha had just been promoted at her bank in Kolkata, and three weddings were coming up in one month. Her cousin Bhupen called. "Everyone's wearing designer outfits this season. You'll look poor if you don't." Bidisha felt a knot in her stomach. Her mother's medical bills had just come in, and her savings were thin. She opened her wardrobe and found two silk saris she'd barely worn. She decided to borrow a necklace from her aunt and spend only on thoughtful gifts. At the first wedding, a cousin whispered about her 'old sari'. Bidisha's face flushed. But at the end of the month, the medical bills were paid on time, and she felt steady instead of anxious.

qa.q: How many weddings were coming up in one month?
qa.a: Three weddings were coming up.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when Bhupen talked about designer outfits?
qa.a: She felt anxious, with a knot in her stomach, because she knew her savings were thin.

qa.q: What choices helped Bidisha separate needs from image?
qa.a: She reused her saris, borrowed a necklace and kept money for her mother's medical bills.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see her choices?
qa.a: Bhupen might think she looked poor, focusing on appearances rather than her real priorities.

grounding: Shows a young woman resisting pressure to spend for status when money is tight.

passage: At the ward office in Gangtok, Neelam sat through her first public meeting about a new parking plan for the market road. Shopkeepers wanted more parking; residents wanted wider footpaths for children and elders. People shouted. Neelam had come only to complain about her lane's streetlight. But her colleague Pema, who volunteered with a residents' group, explained quietly that the council had a fixed budget and had to choose. Neelam listened to both sides. At the end, she stood up, nervous, and suggested staggered parking hours so both could share the road. A councillor wrote it down. She didn't know if it would happen. But walking home, she understood why decisions took so long.

qa.q: What did Neelam originally come to complain about?
qa.a: She came to complain about her lane's streetlight.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel when she stood up to speak?
qa.a: She felt nervous, but she still offered her idea.

qa.q: What made Neelam's contribution constructive?
qa.a: She listened to both sides and suggested a compromise that fit the budget limits.

qa.q: How might the shopkeepers and residents see the problem differently?
qa.a: Shopkeepers focus on parking for business, while residents want safe footpaths for children and elders.

grounding: Shows a young woman learning about policy trade-offs and joining local decision-making constructively.

passage:
Dear Nazia,

You asked why I've started going to the gram sabha meetings when I visit home. Honestly, it started because I was annoyed.

The village wanted a new road, and I thought it was obvious. Then I went. I learned that the same money could either fix the road or repair the school roof. The farmers wanted the road for their trucks. Mothers wanted the roof fixed before monsoon. Both were right.

I didn't have the answer. But I helped write a letter to the district office asking whether a separate scheme could fund the roof. It took three months. They said yes.

I used to think politics was just shouting on TV. Now I think it's mostly listening to people who want different good things.

Suraj

qa.q: What two things could the same money be used for?
qa.a: It could fix the road or repair the school roof.

qa.q: Why did Suraj first go to the gram sabha meetings?
qa.a: Suraj was annoyed and thought the answer about the road was obvious.

qa.q: What did Suraj do that helped both groups?
qa.a: Suraj helped write a letter asking the district office whether a separate scheme could fund the roof, which worked.

qa.q: How might the mothers at the meeting see the roof issue?
qa.a: They want the roof fixed before monsoon so their children stay safe and dry in school.

grounding: Shows a young adult understanding trade-offs in local policy and taking constructive action.

passage: So here's how I, Naveen, got involved. Last year our apartment building in Chandigarh had a fight over water. The corporation announced cuts, and everyone blamed the building committee. I was twenty-four and just wanted to shower in peace. My neighbour Hansa, a retired teacher, suggested we read the corporation's actual notice. Turned out the cuts were because the reservoir was low, not because anyone was lazy. So we did something unusual. We held a meeting, explained the notice, and set a building schedule for washing and storage. Then Hansa and I went to the ward councillor's open hour and asked for a tanker on the worst days. We got two tankers a week. I didn't expect to enjoy civic stuff. But I did.

qa.q: Why were there water cuts, according to the notice?
qa.a: The cuts were because the reservoir was low.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel about civic issues at first?
qa.a: Naveen didn't care much at first and just wanted to shower in peace.

qa.q: What steps turned blame into constructive action?
qa.a: Reading the actual notice, explaining it to neighbours, setting a building schedule and asking the councillor for tankers.

qa.q: How might the building committee have felt before the meeting?
qa.a: They were probably frustrated at being blamed for cuts they didn't cause.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning why a policy decision was made and taking part constructively in local governance.
